parts.text:
Plate tectonics is one of the reasons Earth looks so different from its planetary neighbours.

The movement of enormous

of our planet’s crust builds mountain ranges, triggers earthquakes, shapes our oceans and continents, and helps regulate Earth’s climate and magnetic field over deep time.

This process may also be key to sustaining the kind of long-term

that allowed complex life to evolve. But exactly when it began has been a long-standing mystery.

In new research, we studied chemical fingerprints in more than 1,000 rocks to look for clues – and found clear evidence for when this remarkable

occurred.

Why plate tectonics matters

Many scientists believe plate tectonics provides the long-term stability that keeps our planet life-friendly, unlike tectonically “dead” worlds such as Venus and Mars.

But debate has

over when this process began: has it run throughout Earth’s entire 4.5-billion-year history, or did it “switch on” at some point along the way?

For much of its early history, Earth may have been mostly covered by oceans, without the shifting,

plates that build tall mountains – which in turn erode away, supplying the nutrients to feed marine life.

The question is hard to settle because plate tectonics are very good at destroying the evidence. Where plates collide, some old crust is

back down into the mantle, and the crust that is thrust upward to form mountains also starts eroding away, which erases the geological record.

Often, all that survives are chemical fingerprints preserved in ancient rocks that have endured for

of years, against the odds.

Reading the fingerprints in rocks

In our new study, we studied one such fingerprint.

New continental crust – the ground we stand on – doesn’t always form fresh from crystallising mantle magma. Often it’s made from

older rock that was already sitting inside existing crust.

That process leaves a lasting chemical trace in the new rocks, a bit like the DNA a child inherits from their parents. This is the fingerprint we studied.

In some minerals (

and some sulfide minerals, in our case) this fingerprint can survive largely undisturbed for billions of years.

We analysed over 1,200 rocks, some newly analysed by us, others compiled from earlier studies, from ancient

across Australia, Africa, North America and Europe, spanning nearly four billion years of Earth’s history.

The vanishing signal

reading.title: 主旨、理解与信息定位
reading.instruction: 阅读原文后回答 5 道选择题：1 道主旨、1 道内容理解、1 道段落细节、2 道信息定位。段落细节题以题干指定段落为准。

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarises the overall focus of this article?
options: Chemical evidence in ancient rocks helps scientists date the beginnings of plate tectonics.
Antarctic microorganisms reveal a rich but often overlooked dimension of biodiversity.
New Zealand's distinctive natural history makes a case for a museum devoted to evolution and geology.
A compass works by aligning a magnetised needle with Earth's magnetic field.
questions.explanation: 把标题与全文各段的中心内容连起来判断主旨，避免把同一主题下的其他话题当成本文重点。
questions.evidence: In new research, we studied chemical fingerprints in more than 1,000 rocks to look for clues – and found clear evidence for when this remarkable shift occurred.

questions.prompt: How did the researchers seek evidence for the geological transition?
options: By analysing chemical fingerprints in over a thousand rocks
By tracking the movements of living cranes
